name: Dialpad
tagline: Cloud business phone system with real-time transcription and call assist for sales and support teams.
description: Dialpad is a cloud business phone system that transcribes live calls and produces written summaries for sales and support teams.
pros: Live transcription produces a text record of a call before anyone opens a notes document
Voice, SMS, and team messaging share one business number instead of three separate tools
Positioned for sales and support teams that want call analytics attached to conversations
Admins assign numbers, routing rules, and users from one web console rather than a telecom system
The recorded band of $15-35/mo gives a buyer a starting figure before contacting sales

features.name: Real-time call transcription
features.description: Converts speech to text while a call is still running, so a transcript is ready when the conversation ends. Language coverage is not recorded in this dataset.

features.name: Post-call written summaries
features.description: Condenses what was discussed and agreed into a short recap attached to the call record, so commitments are not left in someone’s memory.

features.name: Outbound power dialer
features.description: Lets a representative work a list of numbers from the same workspace that holds transcripts and recordings. Exact dialer modes are not itemized here.

features.name: IVR menus and call routing
features.description: Greets callers with menu options and hunts across users or queues until someone answers. Multi-site and department routing is configured from the admin side.

features.name: SMS and team messaging
features.description: Business texting and internal chat share the workspace with voice, so a customer conversation can continue on the same number after a call ends.

features.name: Business number administration
features.description: Assigns and reassigns company numbers, extensions, and departments from a web console. Porting timelines are not recorded in this dataset.

features.name: Call analytics and recording
features.description: Call logs, recording, and reporting surface usage patterns for managers reviewing team calling. The dataset does not enumerate the available report types.

features.name: Desktop, web, and mobile apps
features.description: The same dialer and history are available from desktop, browser, and mobile clients, which is what lets a business number follow a user off the desk.

content.title: Dialpad at a glance
content.body: Dialpad is a cloud business phone system. Call control sits in the vendor’s infrastructure, employees dial from a desktop, web, or mobile client, and a pool of business numbers takes the place of an on-site PBX. The layer that separates it from plain hosted telephony is speech-to-text: transcription runs while a conversation is still unfolding, and a written recap follows the call. Our dataset files Dialpad under Communication with a paid pricing model and a recorded band of $15-35/mo. Everything below is drawn from published Dialpad documentation and the fields stored in this repository’s dataset; nobody here used the product to produce this page.

content.title: Transcription on live calls
content.body: For a sales or support conversation, the artifact worth keeping is the text of what was said rather than an audio file nobody replays. Dialpad converts speech to text during the call, so a transcript exists by the time the rep hangs up, and a post-call summary condenses commitments and next steps into a short record. Because the processing happens on the cloud side, the transcript lands in the same workspace as call history and recordings. What this repository does not record is which languages transcription covers, how long recordings or transcripts are kept, or what deletion rules apply — those details need confirmation from the vendor.

content.title: Outbound dialer, routing, and IVR
content.body: The phone side covers the mechanics a buyer actually audits: an outbound dialer for high-volume calling, ring rules that hunt across devices, queue and overflow behavior for support lines, and IVR menus that route a caller to a department before a person picks up. Numbers can be assigned per user, per department, or per location from the admin side, which is what makes a multi-site setup manageable without a telecom contractor. Our dataset records the existence of these controls at a category level only; specific routing logic, queue options, and dialer modes are not itemized here, so they should be checked against vendor documentation.

content.title: Where the dialer earns its keep
content.body: The product shape points at a particular buyer, and this repository’s own alternative listing agrees: Dialpad is described here as messaging with voice intelligence, aimed at sales and support teams that want chat connected to call analytics. These are the situations that match what the product is built to do.
items: Sales teams running high call volumes who want every conversation transcribed without a note-taker in the room
Support desks that need a written record of what was promised during a call
Managers who coach from transcripts and call reviews rather than from memory
Small and mid-sized businesses swapping an on-site PBX for cloud-hosted numbers
Companies that want voice, SMS, and team messaging attached to one business number

content.title: Pricing recorded for Dialpad
content.body: Our dataset records a list price band of $15-35/mo under a paid pricing model, with no free tier in these fields. Plan structure, whether the figure is per user or per line, and any add-on costs beyond core telephony are not captured, so the band should be treated as an entry reference rather than a quote. Buyers weighing Dialpad against meeting-led or messaging-led tools should price the whole headcount, because a phone system licenses every user who needs to place or receive calls. Confirm current list pricing and packaging directly with the vendor before budgeting.

content.title: Pushing call events into other systems
content.body: Like most hosted phone systems, Dialpad is expected to sit beside the tools a company already runs rather than replace them: call events can be forwarded to other applications over published APIs and webhooks, and a call log entry is far more useful when it lands on the customer record it belongs to. This dataset records that an API is available but does not enumerate named connectors, so any specific CRM, helpdesk, or directory integration has to be checked against the vendor’s current marketplace. Directory synchronization and calendar-driven presence are the follow-up questions IT usually raises next.

content.title: Cloud-only deployment and the data path
content.body: The deployment recorded for Dialpad is cloud only, which follows from the design: transcription and call routing happen in the vendor’s infrastructure, so audio leaves the customer network on every call. That is a clean fit for distributed workforces and a poor one for organizations required to keep voice processing inside their own perimeter. This repository records no security certifications, data-residency terms, or retention policies for Dialpad, and none should be inferred from category labels or pricing fields; confirm current documentation and contractual terms with the vendor.

content.title: Limits that follow from the design
content.body: Three limitations follow from what Dialpad is. There is no on-premises deployment path, so air-gapped or strictly local voice requirements end the conversation early. Every user who needs to call is a licensed user, which is awkward for occasional or seasonal phone needs. And the suite is voice-first: teams whose daily work is meetings and channels will find more room in a collaboration-led platform, while organizations wanting contact center depth will be looking at specialist vendors. The dataset’s silence on certifications and transcription coverage compounds the first point rather than offsetting it.

content.title: Alternatives and the verdict on Dialpad
content.body: Within this repository, Dialpad is measured against RingCentral, which carries a broader estate including video meetings, devices, and contact center add-ons, and against meeting-led tools such as Microsoft Teams and Zoom that approach communication from the calendar outward. Telegram sits at the opposite end — free, consumer-shaped messaging with no phone system at all — while Vonage sells communications APIs rather than a ready application. Our dataset carries an overall score of 4.3/5 for Dialpad across 1,360 recorded reviews. The honest read: it fits buyers whose problem is business calling with transcription attached, and fits poorly when the problem is meetings, channels, or developer embeds.

faqs.question: Does Dialpad transcribe calls in real time?
faqs.answer: Yes. Dialpad publishes live transcription during calls plus a written recap afterward. Which languages are covered, and how long transcripts are retained, are not recorded in this dataset, so confirm both with the vendor.

faqs.question: Is Dialpad a phone system or a meeting tool?
faqs.answer: It is a business phone system first: numbers, dialer, routing, IVR, and SMS, with meetings and messaging alongside it. Our dataset records a paid band of $15-35/mo for Dialpad.

faqs.question: Can Dialpad run on our own servers?
faqs.answer: No. The recorded deployment for Dialpad is cloud only, and transcription depends on call audio reaching the vendor’s infrastructure, so there is no local deployment path.

faqs.question: How does Dialpad differ from RingCentral?
faqs.answer: RingCentral sells a wider estate — phone, video meetings, messaging, devices, and contact center add-ons — while Dialpad concentrates on calling with transcription and call analysis for sales and support teams.

faqs.question: What does this dataset leave out about Dialpad pricing?
faqs.answer: It records a band of $15-35/mo and nothing about plan tiers, add-ons, or per-line structure. Treat it as an entry reference and check the vendor’s published pricing for an actual quote.

author: Emily Nakamura
learningCurve: Day-to-day calling is quick to pick up; routing, IVR trees, and reporting configuration are where the real setup time goes.
whoShouldUse: Sales and support organizations that live on the phone and want transcripts and summaries attached to every conversation, plus small and mid-sized businesses replacing an on-site PBX with cloud-hosted numbers.
whoShouldNotUse: Teams whose daily work is meetings and channels rather than calls, organizations that require on-premises voice processing, and buyers who need certification evidence this dataset does not carry.
